query: For a selected high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, what governs whether and how superconductivity emerges in the low-temperature test regime, and why? Propose one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison with the starting state, the observations expected relative to that baseline, the limits over which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: For the (TaNb)HfZrTi high-entropy alloy, applying controlled hydrostatic pressure will reduce the lattice constant, thereby increasing the density-of-states at the Fermi level and enhancing the electron–phonon coupling up to an optimal pressure. This enhancement will lead to an increase in the superconducting Tc relative to the ambient-pressure state, followed by a decrease once over-compression sets in.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast (TaNb)HfZrTi HEA synthesized under ambient conditions, exhibiting its intrinsic superconducting behavior and baseline lattice parameters.
generation.intervention: Apply hydrostatic pressure using a diamond anvil cell across a wide pressure range (from ambient up to approximately 200 GPa), while conducting low-temperature (1–10 K) electrical transport and magnetic susceptibility measurements.
generation.conditions: Low-temperature measurements under well-calibrated hydrostatic pressure conditions; pressure steps should be fine enough to capture non-monotonic changes in Tc without inducing a structural phase transition.
generation.structural_mediator: Pressure-induced lattice compression that modifies interatomic distances and the electronic band structure, particularly affecting the density-of-states at the Fermi level.
generation.mechanism: Under increasing pressure, lattice compression enhances the electron–phonon coupling by increasing the density-of-states at the Fermi level. This improves the conditions for Cooper pairing, raising Tc up to an optimum pressure. Beyond this optimum, further compression degrades the beneficial coupling or over-compresses the lattice, leading to a reduction in Tc.
generation.predicted_outcome: A non-monotonic behavior in Tc as a function of applied pressure: an initial increase relative to the ambient state, reaching a maximum Tc at an intermediate pressure, followed by a decrease if pressure is further increased.
generation.baseline: Superconducting and electronic properties of the as-cast (TaNb)HfZrTi alloy measured at ambient pressure serve as the baseline for comparison.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold over pressure ranges from ambient up to ~200 GPa. Beyond these pressures, potential structural phase transitions or material degradation may occur, limiting the applicability of the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The exact pressure at which maximum Tc occurs and the magnitude of Tc enhancement are uncertain, as they may be influenced by minute compositional and microstructural variations. Additionally, potential unanticipated effects at very high pressures (>200 GPa) add uncertainty to the hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Subject (TaNb)HfZrTi HEA samples to a series of well-controlled hydrostatic pressure increments, starting from ambient up to ~200 GPa, using a diamond anvil cell. At each pressure step, perform low-temperature (1–10 K) electrical resistance and magnetic susceptibility measurements. Complement these measurements with in situ high-pressure X-ray diffraction to monitor the lattice parameters and check for any structural phase transitions.
measurements: Superconducting transition temperature (Tc) derived from zero-resistance and diamagnetic onset measurements
Critical magnetic fields under different pressures
Lattice parameters obtained via high-pressure XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the superconducting transition temperature does not show a reproducible non-monotonic trend (i.e., a distinct increase to a maximum followed by a decrease) as pressure increases, or if structural analysis reveals a phase transition or degradation that accounts for the Tc variations, then the pressure-induced mechanism as stated will be considered falsified.

A sharp drop to a zero-resistance superconducting state is observed at ∼7.7 K (we define TC as the temperature where the resistance changes from a finite value to zero), consistent with the results reported in ref. . Applying a magnetic field on the sample shows that its superconducting transition temperature (TC) systematically shifts to lower temperature (Fig. 1A, Inset), as expected. Temperature-dependent constant-current magnetic susceptibility characterization was also performed for the ambient-pressure sample. As shown in Fig. 1B, a strong diamagnetic response is observed starting at 7.6 K, indicative of a bulk superconducting nature. High-pressure resistance measurements were performed for four samples that were cut from the material used as the standard for the superconductivity at ambient pressure. The electrical resistance measurements for these samples were performed between 4 and 300 K. High-pressure synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements on the (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 HEA were performed at beamline 15U of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility. The results of two independent experiments show that the superconducting HEA does not undergo a structural phase transition up to pressures of ∼96 GPa where the volume is compressed by ∼28% (Fig. 4 A and B and Fig. S1), but its body-centered-cubic (bcc) structure is still maintained. Further, if the change of the volume is linearly extrapolated up to 190 GPa from 60 GPa, the volume is compressed by ∼53%. An analysis of the data (Fig. 4C) shows that the pressure dependence of the superconducting critical temperature TC of the bcc superconducting HEA (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 is quite distinct from those of the bcc superconductors Nb and Ta, which are the major elemental constituents of the HEA material. [The superconducting TC of elemental Ta has been measured to higher pressures than are found in the literature as part of the current study (Fig. S2)]. proposals.intervention: Systematically vary the mixing entropy by partially substituting Mo with a lighter, isostructural element (e.g. V) in small increments (e.g. 5–20% substitution levels)
proposals.conditions: Synthesize a series of CoCrFeNi(Mo1–xVx)0.85 samples and test at low temperatures (down to 1.5 K) under identical cooling and measurement protocols
proposals.structural_mediator: Local random arrangement (disorder) of the constituent elements and the corresponding variation in configurational entropy
proposals.mechanism: Increasing mixing entropy enhances the electron scattering environment, which in the ‘dirty limit’ can modify electron-phonon coupling to favor a conventional isotropic s-wave superconducting state (BCS-type). The hypothesis is that a threshold disorder level from high configurational entropy triggers the emergence of superconductivity by optimizing the balance between pairing interactions and scattering losses
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples with mixing entropy above a specific threshold (higher V substitution) will exhibit a clear superconducting transition (zero resistance and diamagnetism) at low temperature, whereas samples below that level will remain in a normal metallic state. A systematic variation in Tc with substitution level is expected within a limited range (approximately 5–20% substitution) before other adverse effects set in
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach directly tests the mechanistic role of chemical disorder and mixing entropy in initiating and governing superconductivity in HEAs, comparing the superconducting state with the baseline alloy (with lower disorder) and establishing limits for the phenomenon

proposals.material_system: (TaNb)HfZrTi HEA (a five-element alloy that crystallizes in a body‐centered cubic structure)
proposals.intervention: Apply controlled thermal annealing treatments (e.g. 800°C for 1, 5, and 10 hours) to induce subtle short-range ordering while also preparing as-cast (rapidly solidified, highly disordered) baseline samples
proposals.conditions: Post-synthesis heat treatments in an inert atmosphere with cooling rates controlled to preserve microstructural features; low-temperature superconductivity measurements conducted down to 2 K
proposals.structural_mediator: Degree of atomic ordering versus randomness and possible formation of nanometer-scale precipitates or modified grain boundary structures
proposals.mechanism: The thermal treatment induces a controlled reduction in the degree of disorder and can create regions with enhanced electron-phonon coupling. Enhanced local ordering reduces electron scattering in critical conduction pathways, leading to better overlap of Cooper pairs. However, too much ordering may eliminate beneficial disorder effects, so there is an optimal degree of short-range order for superconductivity to emerge
proposals.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples are expected to show a higher superconducting transition temperature and a more robust zero-resistance state compared to the as-cast state. There should be an optimal annealing time beyond which Tc may decrease due to overordering adversely affecting the pairing mechanism
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This proposal provides a controlled comparison between a baseline (highly disordered as-cast HEA) and thermally modified states, directly linking the microstructural evolution (mediator) to the emergence and characteristics of superconductivity

proposals.intervention: Conduct high-pressure experiments using a diamond anvil cell to apply hydrostatic pressures ranging from ambient up to ~200 GPa while monitoring superconducting properties
proposals.conditions: Low-temperature transport and magnetic susceptibility measurements performed under variable pressure conditions, with careful calibration of pressure using standard methods
proposals.structural_mediator: Lattice compression which alters interatomic distances and the density of states near the Fermi level
proposals.mechanism: Pressure-induced lattice contraction is expected to modify the electron-phonon interaction strength and can tune the density of states at the Fermi level. This can either enhance or suppress superconducting pairing interactions, leading to a non-monotonic change in superconducting critical temperature (Tc)
proposals.predicted_outcome: A clear pressure dependence of Tc should be observed – with an initial increase in Tc as pressure optimizes the electron-phonon coupling, followed by a decrease once pressure over-compresses the lattice. This trend should hold up to the pressure limits explored (~200 GPa), and a maximum in Tc would serve as a key indicator supporting the hypothesis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By comparing superconducting properties at ambient pressure (baseline) with those under applied pressure, this approach elucidates the underlying electronic and lattice factors that govern superconductivity in HEAs, along with a falsifiable trend in Tc as a function of lattice compression

proposals.material_system: A computational model of an equimolar HEA (e.g. CoCrFeNiMo-based alloy) with fully random site occupancy
proposals.intervention: Conduct density functional theory (DFT) based electronic structure simulations combined with disorder averaging (using techniques such as the coherent potential approximation) to evaluate electron-phonon coupling as a function of disorder strength
proposals.conditions: Simulations performed at 0 K and extrapolated to finite temperatures relevant for superconductivity (in the range of 1–10 K), varying the simulated degree of atomic disorder (e.g. by varying assumed potential fluctuation amplitudes)
proposals.structural_mediator: Variations in local electronic density-of-states and phonon spectra arising from different configurations of chemical disorder
proposals.mechanism: The model hypothesizes that a critical degree of electronic scattering due to disorder leads to a measurable enhancement of the electron-phonon coupling constant. When the effective scattering rate crosses a threshold, Cooper pairing becomes energetically favorable, and superconductivity emerges
proposals.predicted_outcome: The simulations would predict a distinct threshold disorder parameter value at which the calculated electron-phonon coupling constant and superconducting Tc rapidly increase compared to the baseline simulated by a perfectly random alloy with lower effective scattering. This trend should consistently reproduce known behavior of conventional s-wave superconductors in the dirty limit
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This computational approach provides a first-principles testable mechanistic hypothesis that can be experimentally compared against measured superconducting properties. If the simulation correctly predicts a threshold disorder parameter and associated Tc enhancement, it validates the mechanistic role of electron scattering and coupling in the emergence of superconductivity in HEAs

decision.rationale: Direction B was chosen because it directly tests the influence of pressure-induced lattice compression on the superconducting properties of (TaNb)HfZrTi HEA. Prior evidence from high-pressure studies (e.g., PMC5740615::web::004::results and PMC5740615::web::007::discussion) supports that modifying interatomic distances alters the density-of-states at the Fermi level and the electron-phonon coupling, resulting in a non-monotonic response in the superconducting transition temperature (Tc). This approach provides a controlled baseline (ambient pressure state) versus intervention (applied pressure) comparison with a clear mechanistic link and falsification criterion.
